item.title: Beyond the UAE: Space42’s $1.7 billion bid to conquer new markets
item.dc:creator: Melissa Hancock
item.description: With government clients still accounting for the bulk of its revenue, Space42 is betting on direct-to-device satellite connectivity, AI-driven geospatial intelligence and strategic acquisitions to broaden its commercial appeal and unlock new markets.
item.content:encoded:
In recent years, Abu Dhabi-based Space42 has emerged as one of the region’s most prominent names in space technology and AI, with its achievements helping to establish the UAE as a respected player in the space industry.

Sitting at the intersection of satellite communications, Earth observation and AI capabilities, Space42 uses space-based infrastructure to deliver connectivity and turn satellite imagery into actionable intelligence.

Now, the company is looking to take that model beyond its home market, committing $1.7 billion to new projects.

To date, government contracts have formed the backbone of Space42’s revenue, but it is now looking to expand its customer base, both domestically and internationally, over the next few years.

Currently, 90% of Space42’s revenue is generated in the UAE, with the remaining 10% coming from international markets. Government clients account for approximately 80% of revenue, while commercial customers contribute the remaining 20%.

“Over a five-year runway, we expect those ratios to move toward a 70/30 split on both fronts,” Karim Sabbagh, managing director of Space42, tells me on the sidelines of the Frontier Summit held in Abu Dhabi this week. 

The company’s $1.7 billion capital deployment commitment forms part of a broader strategy to double Space42’s revenue to $600 million by 2030. 

The company generated $260 million in revenue in the first half of 2026, up 15% year-on-year, while netting $18 million in profit. 

According to Sabbagh, the company is considering increasing its $1.7 billion capital plan. “If anything, we may make the plan more ambitious,” he says, adding that any decision would be announced at the company’s annual investor day next month. 

Beyond organic investment, he shared that Space42, is open to acquisitions that would add specific capabilities. While the company operates as a private sector entity, it is heavily backed by Abu Dhabi’s sovereign fund Mubadala, which has $385 billion in assets under management, as well as International Holding Company, a diversified investment conglomerate and Abu Dhabi’s largest listed firm. 

“I think there are going to be opportunities for very complementary capabilities, particularly in geospatial intelligence,” Sabbagh says.

Acquisition targets could include companies that have developed specialized analytical models and established customer bases in areas such as agriculture and critical infrastructure. Such businesses can help transform raw observations into practical insights, from comparing conditions over time to assessing how a situation might evolve.

Last month, Space42 signed a binding agreement with U.S. communications company Viasat to establish Equatys, a shared platform designed to connect smartphones and other devices directly to satellites.

Viasat will be committing $400 million in equity to the venture, while Space42 is committing $600 million, which it sees as central to its ambition to diversify its geographic reach.  

Traditional mobile satellite services have often relied on specialized equipment, including satellite phones. Direct-to-device technology could therefore expand the addressable market considerably.

The platform is expected to launch by 2029, and will initially comprise fewer than 200 satellites, with plans to expand the constellation to 2,800.

According to Sabbagh, Equatys will be able to leverage 400 relationships with mobile network operators across the world.

“The business model is unique because it’s a shared infrastructure in space, which will then allow existing sovereign direct-to-device satellite networks to integrate with our system,” says Sabbagh.

Rather than requiring every country or operator to develop and maintain their own satellite network, the model would allow participants to integrate their systems with a broader infrastructure.

A European, Canadian, or Indonesian direct-to-device network, for instance, could potentially connect to the Equatys infrastructure when operating within its intended territory. The shared network could then help extend connectivity when that national system operates beyond its own area of interest.

The aim is to make better use of satellite capacity that might otherwise sit idle when a system is outside its primary coverage area.

Sabbagh predicts this could transform the space industry from having less than 10 million users of mobile satellite services to being able to reach billions of users.

“We want to truly democratize space-based voice and data services to make them accessible at a price point that’s comparable to the services offered by alternatives delivered through terrestrial platforms,” he added. 

Satellite connectivity currently commands a premium because of its relatively high cost, limiting its accessibility for some users.

There is, however, a transition period to navigate. Space42 expects new services to require time to build subscriber bases, establish commercial packages, and secure adoption, with Sabbagh estimating this could take one to three years.

Space42’s other major differentiator, according to Sabbagh, is its strategy to bring satellite communications, Earth observation, and AI-enabled analysis together within a single business.

As satellites generate growing volumes of data, the challenge is increasingly how quickly that information can be processed and translated into useful intelligence.

AI plays a central role in aggregating observations, identifying objects, comparing changes over time and supporting analysts as they investigate specific questions. Applications could range from assessing the impact of an earthquake by comparing imagery before and after an event to monitoring changes in infrastructure or identifying developments in a sensitive area.

The technology is particularly important when working with synthetic aperture radar, otherwise known as SAR.

Unlike conventional optical imaging, which depends on reflected sunlight and can be constrained by darkness and cloud cover, SAR uses radar signals and their reflections to construct images of the Earth’s surface. This enables observations in conditions where optical imagery may be limited. 

“Many situational awareness requirements arise at night. An optical lens, for example, cannot capture images from 400 kilometres away in the dark,” says Sabbagh.

“Or let’s say that it’s raining, or there’s cloud cover or fumes. SAR doesn’t care about any of this. The radar signal will go in, the reflection will come out, and you’ll be able to derive your intelligence.” 

Future success will require Space42 to turn its technological capabilities, capital commitments and international partnerships into commercially viable services that can compete across markets at scale and at a sustainable cost. 

This story was originally featured on Fortune.com

item.title: Exclusive: AI code-testing startup Blacksmith hits $1 billion valuation as AI-written code surges
item.dc:creator: Beatrice Nolan
item.description: The startup’s valuation has nearly doubled in two months as AI coding tools flood companies with more code than their testing systems can handle.
item.content:encoded:
Blacksmith, a startup that runs the infrastructure companies use to test code before it ships, has been valued at $1 billion following a new $66 million funding round led by Sequoia Capital.

The round, which is Blacksmith’s Series C, comes about two months after the company raised a $45 million Series B led by Peak XV Partners at a $550 million valuation. It brings Blacksmith’s total funding to about $124.5 million.

Blacksmith says more than 10,000 companies now use its platform, up from about 5,000 in August. Customers include well-known startups Granola, Handshake, Supabase and LangChain. At the start of the year Blacksmith ran 5 million validation checks a week; it now runs 90 million. Annual recurring revenue has grown 17x over the same period, according to cofounder and CEO Aditya Jayaprakash, who said revenue is now in the tens of millions. The company said its largest customers spend more than $1 million a year.

Jayaprakash told Fortune that most of the new money will go toward purchasing more computing power. The company has about 40 employees across San Francisco and New York and plans to reach around 75 by the end of the year.

Blacksmith was founded in 2024 by Jayaprakash, and sells what developers call continuous integration, or CI: the automated builds and tests that code has to pass before it can be merged into an existing codebase and deployed. Most companies run those jobs on servers rented from AWS, Google Cloud or Microsoft Azure. Blacksmith instead buys its own machines, tens of thousands of them, according to Jayaprakash, and installs them in data centers around the world. It has writes its own software to run them, including systems that save the repetitive setup work each test run would otherwise redo from scratch.

A new bottleneck

Developers used to spend about half their time writing code and the other half waiting for it to build and pass checks, Jayaprakash said.

AI coding tools like Cursor, OpenAI’s Codex and Anthropic’s Claude Code have made the first half “extremely easy,” he said. “But now the bottleneck has shifted to the second piece, which is: how do I actually validate all this code?”

Even the leading labs are feeling the strain. Anthropic said last month that its own validation workloads grew 25 fold in six months as Claude took over most of its code output.

Blacksmith owns much of its own hardware—it buys its own servers rather than renting them from cloud giants like Amazon—which Jayaprakash says gives the company control over performance, but also exposes the company to the industry-wide shortage of compute and memory. Jayaprakash said capacity planning is one of the hardest parts of the business, because demand jumps every time a stronger model comes out. When Anthropic launched Claude Fable 5 in July, he said, CI volume on Blacksmith rose 40%.

As with many AI coding startups, there’s also a threat that leading AI model vendors—which already focus heavily on coding products—will eventually take over code validation themselves.

Coding agents like Codex and Claude Code can already run a project’s tests as they work, and Cursor launched a product in March that lets companies set up agents to automatically review and test new code. Meanwhile, Microsoft-owned GitHub sells its own hosted machines for running CI jobs. Jayaprakash argues Blacksmith is complementary to what the AI model companies do, because better models mean more code to check. “Usage on us actually goes up,” he said.

This story was originally featured on Fortune.com

item.title: Ken Griffin says Trump’s plan for America First was always doomed to fail: ‘Most people don’t want to live that dream’
item.dc:creator: Eleanor Pringle
item.description: "To be blunt, like, I hate to say it, but I've been right."
item.content:encoded:
When President Trump told the world on “Liberation Day” last year that foreigners had “torn apart our once-beautiful American dream,” his plan to restore it promised “jobs and factories will come roaring back into our country.”

Analysts and business moguls were dubious of the “America First” agenda. Coupled with sweeping tariffs on the entire world, many were concerned that nationalism may result in America ending up alone.

Citadel’s Ken Griffin was among those who weren’t sold on the scheme, and 18 months after Trump’s famed Rose Garden address, the billionaire CEO has declared tariffs a “disaster.”

Griffin suggested the plan to reindustrialize the nation to restore the American dream was flawed from the outset. Speaking at the Citadel Securities Future of Global Markets yesterday. Griffin said: “To be blunt, like, I hate to say it, but I’ve been right. It’s been pro-inflation.”

“It has certainly taken supply chains around the world and severed them. And we’re not going to industrialize efficiently in our country. Unemployment’s low [4.2%], like if you have this dream of an industrialized America, number one is most people don’t want to live that dream. They don’t want to be in factories making Nike’s and T-shirts.”

It’s a phenomenon that analysts have observed trickling through the labor market: Moody’s chief economist, Mark Zandi, noted this summer that native-born unemployment among Americans had begun to rise, based on analysis of a 12-month moving average of seasonally unadjusted data. Part of the reason for this, Zandi told Fortune, is that U.S.-born workers don’t want to take on the jobs historically held by immigrant workers for relatively lower wages.

“It just goes to show how difficult many of these jobs are,” Zandi said. “Native-born workers would take them, but it would require much, much higher wages … [and that] would make it uneconomic for the businesses to actually produce whatever it is they’re doing.”

He added: “These jobs are typically ones that are very difficult, very arduous jobs that require a lot of physical hardship, and the native-born workers just haven’t done these jobs for quite some time and are in no mood to take them now—certainly not at these wages.”

Bring in the robots

Instead, Griffin advocated for robotics—increasingly advanced thanks to artificial intelligence—to carry out U.S. manufacturing of essential goods efficiently. In September, Griffin announced a $3 billion gift to Carnegie Mellon University Miami, to pursue the “next era of American innovation.”

“We want re-industrialized America to be a really industrialized America with robotics running our factories,” Griffin said. “Like, that’s forward-thinking. That’s how our country secures greater independence from the rest of the world on items that are important to our national interests.”

But this suggestion may also divide opinion. The St Louis Fed estimates that approximately 12.6 million Americans are employed in the manufacturing sector, predominantly in electrical and component manufacturing. According to the Bureau of Labor Statistics, the industry made up 7.4% of total employment in 2025 and was expected to contribute 7.2% by 2035.

So while the sector is not as significant to the employment picture as retail, healthcare, or state and local government, it remains a lifeline to millions—which is why Microsoft co-founder Bill Gates suggested a robot tax in an August essay.

“A tax would slow the rush away from human labor a little and raise money for retraining and a stronger safety net,” Gates said, “It would need to be targeted so it does not slow down the purely beneficial uses of AI, like making medicine and education cheaper.”

This story was originally featured on Fortune.com
